","Voter Heather Wagner said affordability was also a big issue for her and that's why she \"went straight Democrat.\"","Wagner said that when she looked at what the Republicans were campaigning on, there was \"nothing with the Republicans I liked.\"","Another Ohio voter, Karen Lynch, said she too supports Brown and also cast her vote for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton.","Like Papa and Wagner, Lynch said she's had it with high prices. that has shifted sharply toward the GOP."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Asked by reporters at his polling location whether he planned to support any Republicans, Sand said he was “actually Democrat, is facing Republican Zach Lahn in a closely watched governor’s race in a state President Trump carried by 13 points in 2024."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Asked what a victory would mean for Iowa’s political direction, Sand resisted drawing broader conclusions."},{},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“That’ll be something that people can debate,” Sand said. “It’ll just mean that I’ve been elected governor.”"},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Sand pointed to support from Republicans and independents who typically vote Republican, saying many want to see “a little bit of balance” restored to state government. He also said connecting with voters through hunting had helped change some people’s perceptions of Democrats."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“I’m not here to be a governor for a party,” Sand said. “Like our yard signs say I want to be the governor for all.”"},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"With rain moving through central Iowa on Election Day, Sand brushed off concerns that the weather could dampen turnout."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“If your supporters are people who are a little bit less excited and the rain turns them away, then that’s a problem for you as a candidate,” he said."}],"text":["As he prepared to cast his ballot in Des Moines on Tuesday, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said he might vote for some Republicans himself, underscoring his cross-party appeal in a state that has shifted sharply toward the GOP.","Asked by reporters at his polling location whether he planned to support any Republicans, Sand said he was “actually not sure yet,” but noted he has previously supported Republican-registered candidates in local, nonpartisan races.","Sand, Iowa’s only statewide elected Democrat, is facing Republican Zach Lahn in a closely watched governor’s race in a state President Trump carried by 13 points in 2024.","Asked what a victory would mean for Iowa’s political direction, Sand resisted drawing broader conclusions.","“That’ll be something that people can debate,” Sand said. “It’ll just mean that I’ve been elected governor.”","Sand pointed to support from Republicans and independents who typically vote Republican, saying many want to see “a little bit of balance” restored to state government. He also said connecting with voters through hunting had helped change some people’s perceptions of Democrats.","“I’m not here to be a governor for a party,” Sand said. “Like our yard signs say I want to be the governor for all.”","With rain moving through central Iowa on Election Day, Sand brushed off concerns that the weather could dampen turnout.","“If your supporters are people who are a little bit less excited and the rain turns them away, then that’s a problem for you as a candidate,” he said."]},"date":{"createdAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:15.507Z","publishedAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:15.507Z","modifiedAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:15.507Z"},"description":{"seo":"As he prepared to cast his ballot in Des Epps, 18, and Jaí Jack, 19, said they needed three tries and 3.5 hours before they were able to cast their first-ever ballots today in South Carolina."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"The two friends said they registered together months ago at their high school but were turned away when they showed up to vote at 3 p.m. in Goose Creek, about 17 miles north of Charleston. They said they were told that their names weren’t on the voter rolls."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“All they said was that, since our names weren’t registered, we couldn’t vote,” Epps, 18, said in a phone interview."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Once outside the precinct, they bumped into a local politician, Democratic state Rep. JA Moore, who urged them to go back inside and request provisional ballots. Those are ballots that are used if there’s a question about a voter’s eligibility."},{},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"They said they went inside a second time — and were turned away again. So, they left."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Finally, after urging from Moore, they said they came back a third time and asked to vote. Epps said that, eventually, poll workers found her name on the rolls, and she was able to cast a regular ballot at about 6:30 p.m, though she said she didn’t get an explanation for why her registration had been so difficult to find."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Jack said she voted by provisional ballot after poll workers still couldn’t find her name on the rolls."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“I don’t understand why I wasn’t registered, when we registered at the same time and place,” she said."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Election officials in Berkeley County, S.C., which includes Goose Creek, did not respond to requests for comment."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Moore praised the young voters’ persistence and criticized the barriers to voting, especially for the state’s Black community. He said a third friend was with Epps and Jack earlier in the day and was also turned away but couldn't return a third time due to work obligations."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"“These girls are heroes,” he said."}],"text":["Baleigh Epps, 18, and Jaí Jack, 19, said they needed three tries and 3.5 hours before they were able to cast their first-ever ballots today in South Carolina.","The two friends said they registered together months ago at their high school but were turned away when they showed up to vote at 3 p.m. in Goose Creek, about 17 miles north of Charleston. They said they were told that their names weren’t on the voter rolls.","“All they said was that, since our names weren’t registered, we couldn’t vote,” Epps, 18, said in a phone interview.","Once outside the precinct, they bumped into a local politician, Democratic state Rep. JA Moore, who urged them to go back inside and request provisional ballots. Those are ballots that are used if there’s a question about a voter’s eligibility.","They said they went inside a second time — and were turned away again. So, they left.","Finally, after urging from Moore, they said they came back a third time and asked to vote. Epps said that, eventually, poll workers found her name on the rolls, and she was able to cast a regular ballot at about 6:30 p.m, though she said she didn’t get an explanation for why her registration had been so difficult to find.","Jack said she voted by provisional ballot after poll workers still couldn’t find her name on the rolls.","“I don’t understand why I wasn’t registered, when we registered at the same time and place,” she said.","Election officials in Berkeley County, S.C., which includes Goose Creek, did not respond to requests for comment.","Moore praised the young voters’ persistence and criticized the barriers to voting, especially for the state’s Black community. He said a third friend was with Epps and Jack earlier in the day and was also turned away but couldn't return a third time due to work obligations.","“These girls are heroes,” he said."]},"date":{"createdAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:07.387Z","publishedAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:07.387Z","modifiedAt":"2026-11-04T00:30:07.387Z"},"description":{"seo":"Baleigh Epps, 18, and Jaí Jack, 19, said they needed three tries and 3.5 hours before they were able to cast their first-ever ballots today in South Carolina.","primary":"Baleigh Epps, 18, and Jaí Jack, 19, said they needed three tries and 3.5 hours before they were able to cast their first-ever ballots today in South Carolina."},"headline":{"seo":"Why it took two first-time voters 3.5 hours to cast ballots in South Carolina","primary":"Why it took two first-time voters 3.5 hours to cast ballots in South Carolina"},"isHeadlineHidden":false,"url":{"primary":"https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/live-blog/midterm-election-results-2026-news-trump-live-updates-rcna605763#rcrd122684"},"teaseImage":null,"authors":[{"type":"person","name":"David Ingram","jobTitle":["Tech Reporter"],"url":{"primary":"https://www.nbcnews.com/author/david-ingram-ncpn890161"},"worksFor":null,"socialMediaProfiles":{"email":null,"facebook":"https://www.facebook.com/davidingramwrites/","instagram":null,"pinterest":null,"snapchat":null,"tiktok":null,"twitter":"@David_Ingram","whatsapp":null,"youtube":null},"longBio":{"markupAndEmbeds":[{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"I am a journalist covering technology for NBC News. After narrowing from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024, Democrats’ edge over Republicans with Latino voters now stands at 16 points."},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Forty-three percent of Latino voters said they identify as Democrats, up from 39% in 2024 but well below the 54% who did so in 2018. Meanwhile, 27% said they now identify as Republicans, down slightly from 2024 but still up from 21% in 2018. "},{},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Latino voters were a key part of the coalition that helped Trump win in 2024, and both parties have competed for their support this year. "}],"text":["The steady erosion of Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters came to a halt this year, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll. After narrowing from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024, Democrats’ edge over Republicans with Latino voters now stands at 16 points.","Forty-three percent of Latino voters said they identify as Democrats, up from 39% in 2024 but well below the 54% who did so in 2018. Meanwhile, 27% said they now identify as Republicans, down slightly from 2024 but still up from 21% in 2018. ","Latino voters were a key part of the coalition that helped Trump win in 2024, and both parties have competed for their support this year. I’m primarily interested in the science of climate change and how it is reshaping our lives. Global warming is forcing challenging decisions about how we live, work and experience the natural world. My goal is to convey the latest science clearly, explain what’s being done to mitigate climate change and assess how communities are adapting to its threats. It’s also crucial to understand inequities and who is being left behind. I’m also interested in scientific mysteries, how policy affects science and new research that inspires wonder and curiosity in any aspect of science. My work at NBC News has allowed me to bike on the surface of the Great Salt Lake, search for crabs in lagoon muck in Washington’s Hood Canal and hike the shores of seaside Maine. I enjoy meeting and learning from scientists, who I’ve found are almost always eager to share their expertise and engage with my curiosities."}]},"primaryImage":null}]},{"id":"rcrd122671","content":{"markupAndEmbeds":[{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Trump criticized Fox News on Truth Social as the first set of polls closed tonight, saying the conservative-leaning network's ratings \"are way down\" because \"because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!\" "},{"type":"markup","element":"p","html":"Trump claimed his numbers are \"better than they have ever been,\" which is false — his approval rating has decreased.
